reviews.plausible_gain_reasoning: The simulated 66.7% is a reduction of fouling detachment stress, not of friction; compliant-coating drag reduction at ship Reynolds numbers has never been reproduced reliably (most careful tests give 0 +/- a few %), so the clean-hull friction benefit versus a standard foul-release coating is ~0-1%.
key_assumption_issues: The metric is fouling detachment stress, while the request's main benefit is frictional drag; the 66.7% gain is not a drag gain.
Shear compliance of a clamped layer is used as proxy for normal pull-off compliance (Kendall) - the numbers scale similarly but the absolute value is not a pull-off stress.
Baseline 0.3 mm/1 MPa is on the stiff/thin side; commercial foul-release systems use 0.15-0.4 mm topcoats at E 0.2-1 MPa over tie-coats, so part of the compliance ratio is baseline choice.
Compliant drag reduction (3%) is asserted from the literature, not modelled; the tuning estimate (1.2 kHz vs 360 Hz) itself shows mistuning.
killer_risks: A 0.1 MPa surface layer is torn and gouged by fenders, tugs, anchor chains and diver cleaning; damaged patches foul and roughen within months.
Hydroelastic instability (static divergence waves) of a soft layer at higher speeds would increase drag sharply.
Silicone-based foul release still accumulates diatom slime at low speed, which costs 5-15% drag and is not addressed.
2 mm of silicone hybrid is 5-7x the material cost of a standard foul-release scheme.

requirement_coverage.name: low_friction_drag
requirement_coverage.reason: No demonstrated friction reduction versus a clean foul-release coating; benefit is only indirect via easier release.

requirement_coverage.name: non_toxic_antifouling
requirement_coverage.reason: Biocide-free foul release with lower release stress; does not stop settlement or slime, relies on speed or cleaning.

requirement_coverage.name: multi_year_seawater_durability
requirement_coverage.reason: Silicone chemistry lasts years, but the very soft top is mechanically fragile; the stiff base helps adhesion only.

requirement_coverage.name: low_consumption_operation
requirement_coverage.reason: Passive, no consumption; repairs of damaged soft areas needed at dockings.

requirement_coverage.name: hull_scale_applicability
requirement_coverage.reason: Sprayable with existing methods, but graded multi-layer 2 mm build is costly and QA of the gradient on 1e4 m2 is hard.

reviews.plausible_gain_reasoning: Apparent slip on hydrated brushes is at most a few nm to tens of nm (often zero within error), giving b+ < 0.01 and no measurable turbulent friction change; clean-vs-clean the gain is ~0%.
key_assumption_issues: Slip length of 50 nm is optimistic; many measurements on brushes give b ~ 0 or effectively negative (the hydrodynamic brush thickness shifts the no-slip plane outward).
Laminar sublayer Couette with fixed edge velocity is a crude proxy; with b+ ~ 0.01 the result is negligible either way.
The mm-scale texture shielding mentioned in the concept is not modelled and would itself add roughness drag.
killer_risks: 100 nm brushes are removed by abrasion and cleaning and hydrolyse in seawater within months, far short of 3-5 years.
Hydrated brushes resist proteins and spores but not barnacle cyprids and tubeworms on a hard PU substrate; macrofouling then sticks strongly to hard PU.
Grafting-from polymerisation on 1e4 m2 of hull is not an industrial process.

requirement_coverage.name: low_friction_drag

reviews.plausible_gain_reasoning: Liquid-infused surfaces only reduce turbulent drag with lubricants less viscous than water (Rosenberg et al. 2016); with a 10 mPa s ester oil the film thins to the texture and acts as a slightly rough or raised wall, so a small drag increase (the -29% of the laminar model is an upper bound for a full free film) is the realistic outcome.
key_assumption_issues: A 10 um free oil film is assumed pinned; in reality it drains and is stripped, so the texture fills or partly empties and the wall condition changes over time.
Effective slip b = h_o(mu_w/mu_o - 1) assumes a flat laminar two-layer Couette flow; interface waves and oil-water emulsion near the wall are ignored.
Supply and loss are computed outside the model; the field does not include consumption.
killer_risks: Continuous discharge of order 100-300 L/day of oil into the sea per ship: environmental and regulatory (MARPOL) showstopper.
Pores and capillaries clog with biofilm and calcareous deposits within weeks when flow stops in port.
Tanks, pumps and a capillary laminate on 1e4 m2 of hull are a ship modification, not a coating; cost is prohibitive.

requirement_coverage.name: low_friction_drag
